extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and readers interested in publication ethics and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplar reporting about detecting and responding to plagiarism discovered during peer review and after publication, with implications for journal procedures, author verification, and use of detection tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check figures for plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers (and journals) should check figures for plagiarism — "we have to check figures for plagiairism [sic]" (as advocated by Elisabeth Bik).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts a case where multiple figures (Figures 2–7) and figure legends were blatantly copied from another group's work. Checking figures is difficult but necessary; computer-based solutions to identify copied figures would be useful and should be freely available to reviewers. Reviewers should actively inspect images/legends, not only the prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) investigation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should "initiate an investigation in accordance with Committee on Publication Ethics guidelines" when allegations of plagiarism arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley "immediately" initiated a COPE-aligned investigation after the allegation. Following COPE steps (investigate promptly, contact authors/institutions, document findings) is presented as the appropriate publisher response to suspected misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retract articles with major unattributed overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles showing a major unattributed overlap with previously published material (figures, legends, or text) are grounds for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The retraction notice cited a "major unattributed overlap between the figures and figure legends" and stated that such publishing practice is against journal policy and Wiley's Best Practice Guidelines on Research Integrity and Publishing Ethics. Retraction is the corrective action when overlap is confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No major unattributed overlap in submitted manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts must not contain major unattributed overlap (text, figures, or legends) with prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unattributed reuse of substantial material—even if images are reused and text is paraphrased—constitutes unacceptable publishing practice and violates journal and publisher integrity policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify authorship and obtain consent from all authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should ensure that all listed co-authors actually participated in and consented to the writing and submission of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The retraction notice quoted some co-authors stating they "did not participate in the writing and submission of the article and gave no consent for publication." The piece highlights risks of impersonation and submissions made on behalf of corresponding authors; journals should require explicit confirmation of authorship/consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication verification of author identities and affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should 'filter' submissions prior to publication by verifying that primary and other authors are members/employees of authentic educational or research entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comment suggested compelling publishers to verify authors' institutional membership/employment as a guard against fraudulent submissions and impersonation. Possible measures include email-domain checks, institutional confirmations, or other identity/affiliation validation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and guard against chatbot/AI-aided paraphrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reviewers should be aware that authors may use AI chatbots to reword lifted text, producing paraphrased but plagiarized prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accused paper appeared to have sections reworded by an AI summarizer. The author warned this will become common unless serious preventive efforts and detection methods are implemented; journals should develop or adopt workflows to detect AI-assisted plagiarism and paraphrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use centralized peer-review records to prevent serial resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: A centralized database or shared peer-review history can identify manuscripts previously rejected for problems (e.g., plagiarism) and prevent serial submissions without addressing reviewer concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter noted Hindawi's central peer review system, which tracks previously rejected manuscripts and requires authors to respond to past reviewer comments before resubmission; adopting similar centralized systems across publishers could reduce repeated resubmissions of problematic papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reviewers with free, computer-based detection tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and publishers should make computer-based solutions to identify copied figures and other plagiarism tools freely available to peer reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments on the article recommended free tools for reviewers to detect copied figures. Making such tools accessible would lower the burden on individual reviewers and improve the likelihood that image plagiarism is caught during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction repeat offenders and institutions with multiple misconduct retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities should consider stronger sanctions (e.g., blacklisting) for authors or institutions with multiple retractions attributable to author misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter urged blacklisting authors and institutions with more than one retraction due to misconduct to reduce tolerance of repeated bad behavior. The article frames this as an enforcement option to deter serial misconduct.
